title: Match Snacks to Appetites
statement:
Each child i has an appetite need[i]. Each snack j has a size size[j]. A child is satisfied by a single snack whose size is at least their appetite. Each child gets at most one snack and each snack goes to at most one child.

Return the largest number of children you can satisfy.

examples.why: Give the 1 to the child who needs 1 and the 2 to the child who needs 2. The child who needs 3 goes without.
Spending the 6 on the child who needs 2 would leave the other child unmatched. Give the 2 there and the 6 to the child who needs 5.
No snack is big enough, and snacks cannot be combined.

hints: Which child is the easiest to satisfy, and which snack should they get?
Give the child with the smallest appetite the smallest snack that is big enough. A bigger snack would be wasted on them.
Sort both lists and walk them with two pointers: move through snacks, and move to the next child each time the current snack fits.

explain.intuition:
Snacks are resources and big snacks are the flexible ones: they fit everybody a small snack fits, and more. So never spend a big snack where a small one would do. The child with the smallest appetite should get the smallest snack that still covers them.

After sorting both lists, that rule becomes a single walk. Take snacks in order of size. If the current snack covers the least hungry child still waiting, match them. If not, this snack is too small for every remaining child, so drop it.
steps: For each snack in sorted order: if c < need.length and the snack is at least need[c], increase c.
Return c, the number of matched children.
pitfalls: Giving each child the biggest snack. That wastes big snacks that a later child needed, as in the second example.
Counting a snack that is too small as used by the child anyway. A too-small snack is simply skipped.

complexity.time: O(n log n + m log m)

solutions.title: Try every assignment
solutions.idea: Recursively decide, for each child, which unused snack they get, or none. Keep the best count.

solutions.title: Sort both and walk
solutions.idea: Smallest snack that fits goes to the least hungry child still waiting. Snacks that fit nobody are skipped.
solutions.time: O(n log n + m log m)

followups: A child may now be given two snacks whose sizes add up to their appetite. Does the greedy still work?
Snacks arrive one at a time and must be handed out on arrival. What is the best strategy, and how far from optimal can it be?
